name: Real-world interviews
summary: Anonymous real-world engineering exercises with guided implementations, tradeoffs, and runnable TypeScript projects.

questions.title: Generate a Mondrian-style Composition
questions.summary: Scope and build a browser-only React application that creates a fresh, bounded composition from constrained randomness.
questions.prompt: Build a static, browser-only frontend that generates a new Mondrian-style composition on initial page load. Do not add a backend or save data. First agree on the characteristics to imitate, choose an MVP achievable during the interview, and leave extension points for deferred rules. The composition must vary between page loads.
questions.sourceNote: Adapted from a privately supplied real interview brief. The originating company and revealing source URL are intentionally withheld.
constraints: Deliver a working browser-only MVP during a normal interview session.
Generate the composition once on initial load; React rerenders must not silently replace it.
Use only orthogonal divisions, bounded rectangles, consistent dark lines, and a restrained off-white, red, yellow, and blue palette.
Keep every generated region inside the composition and prevent unusably small regions.
Make the composition responsive and keep the generator separate from the renderer.
Explain which characteristics were deliberately deferred and how the design could add them later.

evaluation.intent: Agree on priorities, turn the ambiguous visual request into a small set of deliverable requirements, and implement stable geometry. Leave room for richer composition rules without overbuilding the interview MVP. Perfect art reproduction is secondary.
expectedSignals: Names the visual grammar before coding: orthogonal black lines, unequal rectangles, asymmetric balance, a warm light ground, and sparse primary-color accents.
Negotiates a concrete MVP and explicitly defers secondary traits such as merged regions, line hierarchy, texture, historical-period fidelity, and export.
Models generation as a pure or seed-driven transform so geometry can be inspected and tested independently from React rendering.
Constrains random choices with minimum sizes, weighted colors, bounded coordinates, and a fixed amount of work instead of trusting arbitrary Math.random calls.
Generates once per seed and changes the seed only for initial load or an explicit regenerate action, avoiding render-time instability.
Uses semantic controls, a useful accessible label for the visual output, stable keys, and a responsive composition surface.
Discusses how the selected renderer affects precision, readability, testing, export, and future visual rules.
Communicates tradeoffs while implementing and can identify the next highest-value refinement after the MVP works.

acceptanceCriteria.title: Orthogonal visual grammar
acceptanceCriteria.explanation: The composition is made from horizontal and vertical divisions only; diagonals, circles, arbitrary polygons, and decorative gradients would change the requested visual language.

acceptanceCriteria.title: Consistent dark structure
acceptanceCriteria.explanation: Black or near-black lines visibly organize the composition, render above fills where appropriate, and remain consistent enough to read as one system.

acceptanceCriteria.title: Asymmetric rectangles
acceptanceCriteria.explanation: Rows, columns, or subdivisions have meaningfully unequal proportions, producing deliberate imbalance rather than a uniform checkerboard.

acceptanceCriteria.title: Restrained weighted palette
acceptanceCriteria.explanation: Most area remains warm white or neutral while red, yellow, and blue appear as sparse accents; choosing every color uniformly produces visual noise.

acceptanceCriteria.title: Valid bounded geometry
acceptanceCriteria.explanation: Coordinates and dimensions stay inside the canvas, have positive area, respect a practical minimum size, and never overlap unexpectedly.

acceptanceCriteria.title: Stable randomness
acceptanceCriteria.explanation: A composition is created once for a seed and remains stable through unrelated React rerenders; reload or the explicit regenerate control creates the next result.

acceptanceCriteria.title: Responsive and accessible output
acceptanceCriteria.explanation: The artwork scales to mobile and desktop without overflow, the regenerate control is keyboard accessible, and the otherwise abstract visual has an informative accessible name.

acceptanceCriteria.title: Extension seams
acceptanceCriteria.explanation: Palette policy, geometry generation, seeded randomness, and rendering are separated well enough to add merged cells, stronger composition heuristics, export, or repeatable seeds later.

redFlags.title: Hardcodes one painting
redFlags.explanation: A fixed arrangement may look convincing but misses the required refresh-time generation and avoids the core modeling problem.

redFlags.title: Randomizes during render
redFlags.explanation: Calling random generation directly in component rendering causes flicker, changes output after unrelated state updates, and behaves especially poorly under React Strict Mode.

redFlags.title: Uses unconstrained geometry
redFlags.explanation: Independent random widths and positions commonly create overlaps, gaps, negative dimensions, or slivers too small to read, showing that invariants were never defined.

redFlags.title: Mutates the DOM directly
redFlags.explanation: Imperative document queries and element mutation fight React ownership, complicate cleanup, and make the generator difficult to test or reuse.

redFlags.title: Overbuilds before an MVP
redFlags.explanation: Starting with a custom canvas engine, physics, image analysis, or a large dependency stack risks finishing nothing and contradicts the explicit scoping portion of the interview.

redFlags.title: Never states a scope
redFlags.explanation: Silently choosing characteristics prevents interviewer collaboration and makes it impossible to judge whether omissions were intentional or accidental.

redFlags.title: Colors every cell uniformly
redFlags.explanation: Equal-probability primary colors create a noisy mosaic instead of the restrained negative space and sparse accents that define the target grammar.

redFlags.title: Assumes one desktop size
redFlags.explanation: Fixed pixel coordinates without a scaling strategy make the deliverable unusable on the mobile-first product and reveal missing layout thinking.

redFlags.title: Omits accessibility
redFlags.explanation: An unlabeled visual and icon-only regeneration control make the experience opaque to assistive technology even though the required semantics are inexpensive.

redFlags.title: Entangles model and renderer
redFlags.explanation: Geometry hidden inside JSX or CSS string concatenation cannot be validated independently and makes future renderers or composition rules costly.

redFlags.title: Cannot explain tradeoffs
redFlags.explanation: A polished artifact without discussion of renderer choice, deferred rules, or failure modes misses the communication and design dimensions of the rubric.

solutionTracks.title: Weighted CSS Grid
solutionTracks.summary: Generate unequal fractional tracks and a sparse weighted palette, then let CSS Grid own all layout and line spacing.

steps.title: Lock the MVP grammar
steps.explanation: Choose unequal rows and columns, one consistent black gap, a warm neutral ground, and exactly three primary-color accents as the deliverable subset.

steps.title: Make randomness repeatable
steps.explanation: Create a small seeded random function so one seed always yields the same track weights, accent positions, and test result.

steps.title: Generate constrained tracks
steps.explanation: Use bounded positive fractional weights rather than independent pixel positions; CSS Grid then guarantees full coverage without overlap.

steps.title: Bias the palette
steps.explanation: Start every cell as warm white, shuffle valid cell indexes, and place one red, one blue, and one yellow accent to guarantee restraint and variety.

steps.title: Render declaratively
steps.explanation: Map the generated cells to stable grid children and change the seed only on initial load or when the labeled regenerate button is pressed.

solutionTracks.explanation: CSS Grid handles the MVP’s geometry: positive tracks cover the surface, gaps form consistent lines, and cells cannot overlap. The TypeScript generator produces only track weights and color assignments, keeping visual policy testable and React rendering small. Later additions can include row or column spans, palette periods, line weights, or composition scoring while preserving the boundary between generation and rendering.
solutionTracks.acceptanceRationale: This meets the practice criteria with a recognizable, randomized, responsive result, explicit visual scope, and browser-native constraints that prevent invalid geometry. It is quick to build and readable under interview pressure, with stable randomness, a sparse palette, and a generator that can evolve without direct DOM manipulation. Hiring decisions depend on the interviewer and agreed requirements.
tradeoffs: Independent grid cells make the first version read more like a structured mosaic than paintings with selectively merged regions.
One grid-wide gap produces a single line weight; historically inspired variation would require extra metadata or layered lines.
Fractional tracks are excellent for responsiveness but less convenient than SVG coordinates for exact export or geometry inspection.
Guaranteeing one of each accent is visually reliable but less organic than a richer composition-scoring policy.

solutionTracks.title: Recursive Rectangular Subdivision
solutionTracks.summary: Recursively split a normalized rectangle, then render the resulting leaf regions as absolutely positioned React elements.

steps.title: Define normalized geometry
steps.explanation: Represent every region as x, y, width, and height percentages so the model is renderer-independent and automatically responsive.

steps.title: Choose bounded splits
steps.explanation: Split between 34% and 66% of the parent and stop by depth, probability, or minimum projected size so no leaf becomes unusable.

steps.title: Bias the orientation
steps.explanation: Prefer vertical splits for wide rectangles and horizontal splits for tall rectangles, using randomness mainly when the aspect ratio is ambiguous.

steps.title: Assign sparse accents
steps.explanation: Generate neutral leaves first, shuffle sufficiently large leaves, and assign the three primary accents to avoid coloring tiny fragments.

steps.title: Project leaves into the DOM
steps.explanation: Render leaf rectangles with percentage positioning and consistent outlines while keeping the recursive algorithm entirely outside JSX.

solutionTracks.explanation: Binary space partitioning models the composition as a tree of split decisions. Each split preserves its parent boundary, so leaves cover the original rectangle without gaps or overlap. Orientation based on aspect ratio and bounded cuts prevent most slivers; depth and probability limits guarantee finite work. Internal nodes can later carry line weights, locked axes, merge decisions, or composition scores without changing the React renderer.
solutionTracks.acceptanceRationale: This meets the practice criteria with a richer model that remains manageable during an interview. Children exactly partition their parent, so each split’s correctness can be checked locally. It produces more varied region sizes than a uniform grid, constrains randomness, preserves repeatability, and makes deferred composition rules explicit outside CSS. Hiring decisions depend on the interviewer and agreed requirements.
tradeoffs: Absolute-positioned leaves need careful outline treatment because adjacent borders can visually double or reveal subpixel seams.
A binary split tree cannot directly create every possible grid topology without later merging or cross-branch alignment rules.
Recursive code is conceptually richer than the CSS Grid MVP and may be harder to explain if interview time is very short.
Percentage rounding is responsive but can create tiny visual seams at some device pixel ratios.

complexity.space: O(number of leaf regions + recursion depth)

solutionTracks.title: Responsive SVG Geometry
solutionTracks.summary: Generate normalized cut coordinates and render fills first, then crisp structural lines in a responsive SVG viewBox.

steps.title: Choose a normalized coordinate system
steps.explanation: Use a 100 by 75 viewBox so the generator works in stable units while the browser scales the final SVG responsively.

steps.title: Generate minimum-safe cuts
steps.explanation: Produce positive weighted segments and normalize their cumulative positions, guaranteeing complete coverage and avoiding nearly coincident random coordinates.

steps.title: Build cells from adjacent cuts
steps.explanation: Every neighboring x and y pair defines one valid non-overlapping rectangle whose width and height are positive by construction.

steps.title: Assign controlled color
steps.explanation: Leave the field neutral and place exactly three shuffled accents, keeping color policy independent from coordinate generation.

steps.title: Draw structure last
steps.explanation: Render colored rectangles before the horizontal and vertical line elements so joins remain crisp and line thickness stays visually consistent.

solutionTracks.explanation: SVG maps the geometry directly to pixels. Normalizing weighted segments produces sorted cuts that cover the viewBox and form valid rectangles. Separate fill and line layers avoid doubled borders and support additional line rules. The geometry can be unit tested, serialized, downloaded, animated, or scored without layout measurements. The viewBox handles responsive scaling.
solutionTracks.acceptanceRationale: This meets the practice criteria with precise invariants and a concise browser-native renderer. It separates geometry, palette, and drawing order, produces stable seeded output, scales across devices, and offers the most direct path to export or advanced line rules. Explain the additional SVG concepts within the agreed MVP scope. Hiring decisions depend on the interviewer and agreed requirements.
tradeoffs: SVG introduces coordinate and drawing-order concepts that may be more machinery than a CSS-only MVP needs.
A full row-by-column cut model remains grid-like until later logic merges cells or terminates selected lines early.
Very thick responsive strokes may need vector-effect or breakpoint tuning if exact screen-space thickness matters.
Large compositions would create many SVG nodes, although the interview-sized region count is comfortably small.

questions.title: Partitioned In-Memory Event Log
questions.summary: Design global IDs, indexed per-key reads, independent consumer cursors, and whole-key rebalancing for millions of events.
questions.prompt: Implement an in-memory event log with several simulated nodes. append(key, value) returns a globally ordered ID, beginning at zero. Every event for the same key belongs to one node. read returns all keys in global-ID order; readKey/read_key returns one key while preserving global IDs. Both start at an inclusive global offset and return a bounded page. Add a node without losing events or changing IDs, and discuss automatic rebalancing. Explain concurrency and memory limits when a user has millions of events. Read the companion lesson for a review of a candidate attempt and clarification questions.
questions.sourceNote: Original anonymous practice adaptation of a user-supplied interview prompt and candidate attempt. The source company and interviewer are not identified.

examples.input: append(user-1, click); append(user-2, view); append(user-1, purchase)
examples.explanation: Per-key results retain global IDs; they are not renumbered.
Offset 1 is inclusive and absent from this key. Seek the next greater ID rather than indexing the key array at position 1 by assumption.

constraints: Practice assumptions: one in-memory coordinator, append-only storage, inclusive offsets, default page limit 100 and allowed limits 0–10000. Missing keys and offsets beyond the tail return empty pages.
No persistence, deletion, retention, cross-process locks, duplicate-request suppression, or real network transfer is implemented.
A reader owns its own cursor; nextOffset is the next global ID it may read. A far-future offset remains pending as new events arrive.
Adding a node moves at most one whole-key bucket by reference. The optional automatic policy uses event counts, a cooldown and a cap; one hot key cannot be split.
TypeScript IDs are primitive bigint and must serialize as decimal strings for JSON. Python uses int. Payloads are stored by reference.

diagrams.title: Publication, ownership, and independent readers
diagrams.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  W[Concurrent callers] --> C[Single coordinator / lock]
  C --> G[Global ID index]
  C --> D[Key ownership directory]
  D --> A[Node 0: whole-key stores]
  D --> B[Node 1: whole-key stores]
  R[Consumer A cursor] --> A
  S[Consumer B cursor] --> A

evaluation.intent: Clarify offset semantics, preserve publication and ownership invariants, then choose a seek structure that supports bounded linear reads. Explain where a one-process simulation stops providing distributed-system guarantees.
expectedSignals: Trace interleaved IDs 0, 1 and 2 before selecting a data structure.
Separate the writer nextId from per-key physical positions and each consumer nextOffset.
Seek once, read only the requested page, and account for index and payload memory.
Keep allocation and index publication atomic within the stated concurrency model.
Explain hot-key limits, migration ownership, and why real Kafka offsets are partition-local.

acceptanceCriteria.title: Correct offsets and pages
acceptanceCriteria.explanation: All results have original global IDs in ascending order, inclusive starts, enforced limits and defined empty results.

acceptanceCriteria.title: Independent resumable reads
acceptanceCriteria.explanation: Two consumers do not overwrite each other; cursors survive same-process key movement and appends after reaching the tail.

acceptanceCriteria.title: Whole-key ownership
acceptanceCriteria.explanation: Each key appears on exactly one simulated node; adding a node preserves every event and total counts.

redFlags.title: Treats a local index as a global ID
redFlags.explanation: Filtering by the callback index or slicing at the global offset skips valid events for interleaved keys.

redFlags.title: Promises constant-time arbitrary seek with only a linked list
redFlags.explanation: A next pointer supports traversal after locating a position. An unindexed offset still needs a search.

redFlags.title: Confuses IDs with publication
redFlags.explanation: Atomic ID allocation alone does not publish payload and all indexes atomically across independent workers.

solutionTracks.title: Indexed arrays and binary search
solutionTracks.summary: The first choice under interview time pressure: append to ordered arrays, seek once, then read forward by position.

steps.title: Pin the observable contract
steps.explanation: Use IDs 0 and 2 for one key and ID 1 for another. Offset 1 for the first key must return ID 2. Agree on inclusive offsets, bounded pages, same-key ownership, and a single-process coordinator.

steps.title: Make publication indivisible
steps.explanation: Allocate one global ID and update the key store, global index and node count in one operation. TypeScript stays synchronous in one agent; Python holds one RLock across the operation. Invalid arguments must not consume an ID.

steps.title: Seek to the first qualifying ID
steps.explanation: Write lower-bound binary search over event.id, not the array index. Its invariant is that all positions before lo are below the requested global offset. After locating the start, walk at most limit entries without filter or slice.

steps.title: Keep each consumer independent
steps.explanation: Open one cursor per reader. Seek once, then retain its physical position. Return at most limit entries and advance nextOffset to the last returned global ID plus one. An empty read preserves its offset; a later append remains readable.

steps.title: Move a whole key and verify boundaries
steps.explanation: Add an ownership map for each node. Move a bucket object and update its owner together; existing cursor references remain valid in this shared heap. Test missing keys, gaps, exact boundaries, two readers, appends after exhaustion, and migration. State that real network migration needs a separate protocol.

solutionTracks.explanation: Appending global IDs in increasing order also orders each key array. Lower bound finds exactly the first event whose ID is at least the offset, including offsets absent from that key. The cursor increments only its own array position, so sequential pages neither repeat nor skip events. The separate global array uses a dense global ID as its index; conversion to number occurs only after read has bounded the ID by the stored length.
solutionTracks.acceptanceRationale: The code returns global IDs, provides ordered global/per-key bounded reads, keeps readers independent, and moves whole-key ownership without changing IDs. Optional automatic growth uses an event-count threshold, cooldown and node cap. These are one-process simulation guarantees, not a distributed durability or throughput claim.
tradeoffs: Choose this during a short interview: it is easy to implement and explain. Arrays provide compact reference storage relative to a link object per event.
A page allocates O(r) result references; it does not copy the entire suffix. A bounded slice after a binary search would also be O(r), if the interviewer permits it.

The global and per-key arrays retain references to the same event, not deep payload copies. JS flat arrays have a finite length limit; this teaching version rejects 2^32 - 1 stored global events. RAM can run out much earlier.
Payloads are caller-owned references: event metadata is frozen, but nested payload mutation is not prevented. Agree on copying/serialization and its cost for a real API.

All variants serialize publication at one coordinator. A hot key cannot be split while the ownership requirement holds. Automatic growth estimates counts, not bytes, and cannot promise balanced capacity.

complexity.time: First per-key page O(log(m + 1) + r); later cursor pages O(r + 1). Global read O(r + 1). Existing-key append amortized O(1), excluding growth checks; a new key scans P nodes. Each scheduled growth check or addNode costs O(P + Kd), scanning the busiest node's Kd keys. A far-future cursor can additionally scan newly arriving events below its requested offset once each.
complexity.space: O(N + K + P) retained event/index metadata plus payload bytes, O(r) result references per page, and O(1) state per open cursor; blocks/anchors add O(N/B) metadata. No payload deep copies.

python.explanation: Copy this complete Python 3.10+ program to solution.py and run python3 solution.py. Integer IDs stay exact. RLock protects allocation, both indexes, reads, cursor movement and node migration across threads in this process; do not rely on the GIL for a multi-step invariant. Reads build a bounded page under the lock, then release it before the caller processes results. This lock does not coordinate separate processes.

complexity.time: First per-key page O(log(m + 1) + r); later cursor pages O(r + 1). Global read O(r + 1). Existing-key append amortized O(1), excluding growth checks; a new key scans P nodes. Each scheduled growth check or addNode costs O(P + Kd), scanning the busiest node's Kd keys. A far-future cursor can additionally scan newly arriving events below its requested offset once each. Python int arithmetic/comparison and TS bigint costs grow with ID bit length; these bounds treat IDs as bounded-width.
complexity.space: O(N + K + P) retained event/index metadata plus payload bytes, O(r) result references per page, and O(1) state per open cursor; blocks/anchors add O(N/B) metadata. No payload deep copies.

solutionTracks.title: Linked chains with sparse anchors
solutionTracks.summary: Keep a next pointer per key event and index every Bth link so an arbitrary offset does not require walking from the head.

steps.title: Pin the observable contract
steps.explanation: Use IDs 0 and 2 for one key and ID 1 for another. Offset 1 for the first key must return ID 2. Agree on inclusive offsets, bounded pages, same-key ownership, and a single-process coordinator.

steps.title: Make publication indivisible
steps.explanation: Allocate one global ID and update the key store, global index and node count in one operation. TypeScript stays synchronous in one agent; Python holds one RLock across the operation. Invalid arguments must not consume an ID.

steps.title: Index occasional links, then follow next
steps.explanation: Append at the tail in constant work and add an anchor every B events. Binary-search the last anchor with ID at most the offset; walk forward to the first qualifying event. Keep the last visited link so a drained cursor can observe a later tail append.

steps.title: Keep each consumer independent
steps.explanation: Open one cursor per reader. Seek once, then retain its physical position. Return at most limit entries and advance nextOffset to the last returned global ID plus one. An empty read preserves its offset; a later append remains readable.

steps.title: Move a whole key and verify boundaries

Test missing keys, gaps, exact boundaries, two readers, appends after exhaustion, and migration. State that real network migration needs a separate protocol.

solutionTracks.explanation: Each link belongs to one key and points to the next event for that key. Anchors are ordered because global IDs increase. Starting at the preceding anchor cannot miss the first qualifying event and needs at most one anchor interval of skipped links. After seeking, following next emits only that key in order. A remembered tail link connects an exhausted reader to later appends without restarting at the head.

Optional automatic growth uses an event-count threshold, cooldown and node cap. These are one-process simulation guarantees, not a distributed durability or throughput claim.
tradeoffs: Use this to discuss cursor traversal when the interviewer asks about a linear read. A bare linked list alone would still need O(m) arbitrary seeking; the sparse anchors are essential.
This is not automatically faster or smaller than an array. Every event adds a link object/pointer, with worse locality and allocator/GC overhead. The anchor index uses O(m/B) references.
Retaining a link in a slow consumer can retain the rest of a chain. Retention and invalidation rules are deliberately outside this append-only example.
Payloads are caller-owned references: event metadata is frozen, but nested payload mutation is not prevented. Agree on copying/serialization and its cost for a real API.

solutionTracks.title: Segmented logs with indexed blocks
solutionTracks.summary: Append into bounded blocks, search block boundaries, then keep a block-and-slot cursor for sequential reads.

steps.title: Pin the observable contract
steps.explanation: Use IDs 0 and 2 for one key and ID 1 for another. Offset 1 for the first key must return ID 2. Agree on inclusive offsets, bounded pages, same-key ownership, and a single-process coordinator.

steps.title: Make publication indivisible
steps.explanation: Allocate one global ID and update the key store, global index and node count in one operation. TypeScript stays synchronous in one agent; Python holds one RLock across the operation. Invalid arguments must not consume an ID.

steps.title: Locate the block and the slot
steps.explanation: Use the last ID in each nonempty block as its ordered fence. Binary-search the first fence at least the offset, then lower-bound within that block. Keep block and slot through page reads. If a cursor opens beyond the tail, retain the partially filled final block so future appends are not skipped.

steps.title: Keep each consumer independent
steps.explanation: Open one cursor per reader. Seek once, then retain its physical position. Return at most limit entries and advance nextOffset to the last returned global ID plus one. An empty read preserves its offset; a later append remains readable.

steps.title: Move a whole key and verify boundaries
steps.explanation: Add an ownership map for each node. Move a bucket object and update its owner together; existing cursor references remain valid in this shared heap. Test missing keys, gaps, exact boundaries, two readers, appends after exhaustion, and migration. State that real network migration needs a separate protocol.

solutionTracks.explanation: Blocks never change order and older full blocks never change membership. Their final IDs increase, so the first block ending at or after the offset contains the first possible answer. A second search chooses its first qualifying slot. Sequential reads cross each block once. The global directory divides a bigint ID into block number and small slot; it never converts the entire ID to a JavaScript number.
solutionTracks.acceptanceRationale: The code returns global IDs, provides ordered global/per-key bounded reads, keeps readers independent, and moves whole-key ownership without changing IDs. Optional automatic growth uses an event-count threshold, cooldown and node cap. These are one-process simulation guarantees, not a distributed durability or throughput claim.
tradeoffs: Use after the indexed-array baseline when asked about millions of events, allocation growth, or future retention. Fixed blocks offer a natural unit for snapshots or eviction, but neither is implemented here.
Block size trades allocation frequency against wasted space in partially filled blocks. Small blocks ease boundary testing; the default is 1024 references, not 1024 bytes.
The global directory remains centralized metadata and payloads remain in RAM. Bigint block keys avoid unsafe numeric conversion; they do not remove memory limits or supply durable storage.
Payloads are caller-owned references: event metadata is frozen, but nested payload mutation is not prevented. Agree on copying/serialization and its cost for a real API.
